body: The standard Japanese Google car is usually black and white and uses a low-cam with a larger blur and lower perspective. Only Switzerland consistently uses low-cam too, while Sri Lanka has occasional use; the car is always blurred in Switzerland.
Japan drives on the left hand side of the road.

Japanese writing combines three systems: kanji, borrowed from Chinese, and two syllabaries, hiragana and katakana. Formal texts mainly use kanji and hiragana, with hiragana being simpler and softer in shape than kanji. Learning these scripts aids in region guessing through frequent terms and names.
Katakana is primarily used for loan words and commonly appears in commercials. Its characters are generally simpler and more geometric compared to the artistic forms of hiragana and kanji.

Recognizing common kanji in place names and cardinal directions helps locate cities and prefectures quickly; wards are easier if the city is known, towns harder. Most kanji have alternative pronunciations.
Japanese architecture features a variety of distinct styles, from traditional country houses and regional designs to modern city buildings and coastal reinforced structures.
Japan mainly uses round concrete poles with screw-like extensions, often featuring electrical plates, guy-wires, and pole reflectors, making them important for region guessing.
In Japan, pole reflectors are typically short and do not reach the ground, featuring common patterns like yellow vertical stripes, yellow diagonal stripes, and white vertical or diagonal stripes.
Japan uses a standard short white licence plate with green text, and a short yellow plate with black text for "light automobiles" or Kei Cars.

Japan has three common road line variations: white solid outer lines with dashed white middle lines, white solid outer lines with solid yellow middle lines, and white solid outer lines with yellow and white middle lines. Yellow outside lines are never used in Japan.
Japan typically uses simple white bollards with circular reflectors on top, though some are black or have other extensions. They may also display the city or prefecture name in kanji.
Japan generally uses these simple, white guardrails.

Prefecture roads in Japan use distinctive hexagonal-shaped shields, often with the prefecture name in kanji below the road number. Variations of these shields appear on prefectural highway shields, directional intersection signs, and small arrow signs.
Common Japanese infrastructure includes a unique stop sign, distinctive school pedestrian crossings, and characteristic traffic mirrors.
Retaining walls can be an excellent clue for Japan in rural areas with little to no information.
Area codes are common nationwide, increasing to the south. Codes ending with 0 often are not regional, e.g., 0120.
Every Japanese region features a distinct plate design on utility poles.
Pole reflector pads vary by region in Japan.
Japanese prefectures can be narrowed down by the style of road diamonds.
Most Japanese prefectures have unique stickers on signposts.
Most regions have unique guy wires. Only the most consistent are mapped.
An orange arrow may be found above the top pole plate in Chugoku.
Orange and black bands wrapped around poles are often in Shikoku.
Pole attachments with approximately 120-degree angles are common in Kansai; some may have angled downward attachments.
Smaller 90-degree angle attachments appear frequently on poles in Shikoku.
Hokkaido electrical poles have either a plus-shaped bar or transformer on two bars; multiple transformers mounted on a square are rare there.
Tohoku transformers often have square holding brackets, zigzag bars, and the Tohoku Electrical Company logo, mounted on plates or squares.
Kanto transformers have two or three insulators, mounted on wooden or round plates with T-shaped bars.
Hokuriku transformers have thin metal bar attachments with small clamp-shaped insulators; Niigata has Tohoku designs instead.
Chubu transformers have painted yellow numbers and black tap connectors, attached using large triangle and horizontal bars or thin metal brackets.
Kansai transformers have straight or zigzag bars on the bottom of a square, with transformers mounted on sides; occasionally on vertical bars.
Chugoku transformers have a cross-shaped bar in the middle of the pole, sometimes with a full triangle mount and white stickers with red numbers.
Shikoku transformers also have cross-shaped bars mounted by half triangles, with hat-shaped horizontal insulators and white stickers with black numbers.
Kyushu transformers have straight bars on the pole side with three insulators, oriented 180 degrees apart.
Okinawa transformers have T-shaped bars mounted on opposite sides of poles.
Grey insulator-like blocks through which wires pass appear in Chubu, Kansai, Chugoku, Shikoku, and rarely Hokkaido.
Pole tops with four thick bars and a circle are common in Chubu.
Tent-shaped pole tops with two filled sides are typical in Hokuriku.
Four thin skinny bar pole tops are common in Chugoku.
In Kanto, tuning fork pole tops have a long top bar with horizontal bars below.
Chubu tuning fork pole tops have a short top bar with horizontal bars below.
Kansai tuning fork pole tops have a thin wire with horizontal bars below.
Hokkaido features an infrastructural arrow to mark shoulder lines under snow, with several rare variations found mostly in Hokkaido and Aomori.
Flat white bollards with separated orange reflectors appear on Kyushu and Yamaguchi; in Hokkaido similar bollards have orange reflectors on both sides.
Some Shikoku bollards feature black stripes beneath the reflectors attached to guardrails or walls.
Tohoku has thick white bollards with octagonal reflectors and yellow stripes, sometimes rectangular tops and black versions; often placed on highways or expressways.
Akita features bollards similar to Tohoku, but with two yellow stripes beneath the reflector.
Toyama’s bollard has one reflector, is extendable, with a red stripe beneath it; variations with a second reflector or yellow stripes are different bollards.
Okayama has bollards with octagonal reflectors, red stripes underneath, and a sloped base-to-reflector connection.
Aomori’s bollards have two yellow stripes, a single circular reflector, and are extendable; sometimes only one thick strip is present.
Tohoku striped bollards, common in Akita, have thinner top halves and no reflectors, covering original bollards.
Northern Chugoku has basic snow poles with thin extended or contracted tops; also found sparingly in Iwate.
Green guardrail bands are common in Oita and Miyazaki but appear throughout Kyushu.
Yellow guardrails are distinctive to Yamaguchi Prefecture.
Chevron-like stickers, usually white or orange, appear on guardrails mostly in Hokkaido; found on guardrail ends, metal posts, and bridges.
Red and yellow striped guardrail ending stickers are common across Chugoku but rare in Yamaguchi; rarely found in Niigata.
Vertical traffic lights are in Hokkaido and NW coast, horizontal traffic lights are elsewhere.
Black signs with two yellow circles are found in Kagawa, including stacked or narrow top variations.
Kerosene tanks (“Claymores”) are common in northern and mountainous prefectures, especially abundant in Hokkaido.
Hot water, gas, and propane tanks occur more frequently in northern or mountainous areas, with variations including covered, exposed, cylindrical, and circular tripod tanks, mostly in rural areas.
“Shosetsu” snow prevention roads, using tiny circles to heat pavement and clear snow, are mainly in northwest coastal prefectures.
Cycling routes in Ehime have white outer and blue inner lines, predominantly along coasts; exceptions exist but are rare.
Distinctive red-tiled roofs are common in Chugoku, especially Hiroshima and Shimane prefectures.
Roof styles change from tiled in the south to flat or level in the north to accommodate heavy snow; northern houses often have ladders for snow clearing.
Okinawa is recognized for white concrete buildings with flat roofs.
Cabbage is abundant in Hokkaido and some northern prefectures, growing often roadside with larger leaves than southern Japan; also found in Sakhalin, Russia (without low-cam).
Green tea plants grow in hedged rows, often protected by fans mounted on poles to prevent frost; majority produced in Shizuoka and Kagoshima prefectures.
Rice production is mainly north of Tokyo, starting as green grass-like growth, turning to brown husks when mature; commonly grown in flooded beds, mainly in Chubu, Kanto, Tohoku, and Hokkaido.
Japanese White Birch grows mainly in Chubu and Hokkaido, less in Tohoku; used to assist region guesses. Japanese Beech differs by grey, spotted bark.
Bamboo grows more often in southern Japan and decreases northward; use as supporting info for region guessing.
Chinese Silver Grass (Kyushu grass) is abundant in Kyushu and common in some northern prefectures; use with other info for clear distinction.
Sugarcane is nearly exclusive to southern Kyushu and Okinawa islands.
Hokkaido has very limited snow and winter coverage; guessing there is best done cautiously. Remaining coverage mostly in southern half.
Japan is mountainous, but Nobi and Kanto plains are notable flat areas and important for region-identification.
Okinawa is recognizable by Shisa guardian lions and specific house plaques with characteristic colors and shapes.
Red-soiled agricultural fields are common on southern islands, especially Miyakojima and Ishigaki in Okinawa.
Mount Fuji, Japan's tallest mountain, features a gradual incline and often snow-covered summit, visible from afar for region guesses.
Tokyo city has a distinctive manhole cover design with a five-petal flower surrounded by many small circles.
Cyrillic script appears on signs in Wakkanai and Nemuro cities, northern Hokkaido.
Artistically painted poles resembling birch trees are unique to the city of Date in Hokkaido.
There are many types of trekkers and tripods spanning multiple prefectures. Due to the volume of info, it's recommended to consult a dedicated resource for details.
